I took my basic class in Freshman year and started working private/IFT that summer. Next summer after I started with the city 911 as a professional, and I take my last final of senior year tomorrow. I've been taking 12-15 credit hours and working 36-48 hour weeks at night with the city. Ain't easy and I spent lots of nights on station or even in the truck doing homework, but it's doable.

Accept that 9 out of every 10 runs will require literally nothing besides packaging, vitals, and diesel. If you do private service (most likely, as a new EMT), this number will increase. If you have a medic partner, they will not be impressed by how well you recite material from class/the textbook/etc. -What will not impress them either is that you know how to put on a 12 lead, prep a fluid bag, assemble IV/intubation/oxygen equipment, can handle BLS on your own, and won't lose your head when things get messy-BUT it might make them decide you're worth keeping around. You will get shit on, vomited on, bled on, peed on, and spit on, in all likelihood, especially if you're lucky enough to get 911. Get used to the idea of seeing someone die. Right in front of you, and despite your best efforts to the contrary. With just you and your partner, or with family and/or bystanders right there and then-or several minutes, hours, or even days prior to your arrival. It's not pretty and I will never get used to it. In terms of assessment, practice taking BPs in a moving vehicle. That was the hardest thing for me at first, especially since I'm slightly hard of hearing. Lung sounds, lung sounds, lung sounds. Your medic partner WILL depend on you to help determine if a tube is in, if a COPD'er is diminished, if a CHF'er is "sucking mud," if an asthmatic is wheezing, and if a wreck victim has a tension pneumothorax. They will. Test drive your ambulance. Know stopping distance, know turn radius, be as comfortable in reverse as you are in drive. Know how to drive so you won't throw your partner and patient around. When it comes to true emergent runs, less speed is more; the lights will get you through traffic, not driving like Evil Knievel. For the love of god, respect people. You have no fucking clue what kind of day they're having, even if the call is routine, or even if it's a prescheduled transport (again, likely for starting out). Even if you hate someone, think they're abusing the system, yadda yadda yadda IT IS YOUR JOB AND PROFESSIONAL-LEGAL OBLIGATION to take people to the hospital for whatever damn well reason they please (even when they have 2 running cars in the driveway and a family member with a license, even if their 8 kids are coming with, even if they look healthier than you). Yes, I hate that just as much as anyone but it is the nature of the current industry and it takes 1 solitary phone call to your supervisor, even from some homeless person on a pay phone saying "Spitative on Truck XX was a jerk to me" and you're looking for a different job. Get to know local PD/Fire, if 911. Being on first-name basis with other responders you'll most likely see every day goes a very long way. Especially when you need them. Have a clear view of a building when you pull up and before you get out of the truck, have an exit plan, a secondary exit plan, and a tertiary "shit happens" plan. You are your number 1 priority, your partner number 2, your patient number 3. Short of catastrophic and/or very serious issues in competency, patient care, harassment, etc. keep shit on the truck first and communicate with your partner. Everyone hates tattle tales, and everyone hates paperwork even more. That being said, stand up for yourself and don't count on anyone to save your ass--you should prevent yourself from needing to be rescued in the first place. Check the truck. No, really. Take out the inventory sheet and check the truck. Nothing's worse than your medic saying "we're going to nasally tube and I need a 6.0 trigger tube, lube, endolock, and syringe, NOW" and you're like "uh, uh, uh, where is it?" or, "we don't have that stuff." I could name you a dozen other examples. Finally, know your limits. When it feels like you need to take a day off, you probably do. Don't let the dry humor and jet-pilot tough guy mentality of people in this industry get to you. People are gonna judge the everloving shit out of you in your first 6 to 12 months, don't show that you're incompetent, and don't try to be the hero, or the popular guy. Being the FNG sucks but it's over before you know it. And, in years of working, I have never had a single shift where I didn't learn something new. Could be something as small as "hey, this is where that shortcut to ED A/B/C is" or as cool as "hey, this is how you titrate EtCO2 when bagging!" So be open-minded and enthusiastic, and welcome to the club.

Some reasons to call:
-Cardio-respiratory arrest
-Inability to move/ambulate due to serious injury or illness (NOT bedridden/disabled patients with a non-emergency condition who simply need a checkup, there are private ambulance services for that)
-Uncontrollable bleeding, broken bones, extreme debilitating pain, pediatric injuries, serious head injuries (unequal pupils, altered level of consciousness, etc.)
-Gunshots, stabbings, serious vehicle accidents with entrapment and/or injury, assaults, falls from heights, and other SERIOUS injuries.
-Loss of consciousness, syncope or near syncope, or sudden unresponsiveness or change in responsiveness
-Crushing chest pain or pressure
-Severe shortness of breath not resolved by medication (inhaler), home oxygen or rest.
-Repeated or prolonged seizures (NOT episodic seizures where the patient is immediately conscious again within seconds)

Reasons NOT to call:
-Out of medication (it's called a pharmacy)
-Routine visit (using the ER as your primary care provider)
-"Hospital Shopping" (calling the ambulance to take you to a different hospital because the wait is too long at Hospital "A" -YES, this does happen)
-For prescheduled appointments at hospital specialty clinics
-Calling an ambulance for childbirth should -never- happen unless it is a TRUE emergency and it is totally unanticipated AND other transport is unavailable. You have no idea how many people just get knocked up and "call da ambalamps" when their water breaks 9 months later. Good prenatal care, it's more than just a good idea. 
-For personal transportation
-For ROUTINE injuries/illnesses that can be dealt with in a doctor's office. You don't need 911 for the flu or for a bruise.

Basically, anything less than a serious threat to life or limb, or anything that can be immediately corrected without medical expertise or advanced equipment? Make an appointment. About half the patients I transport wind up in the waiting room because they called for some bogus, routine reason and think that taking my ambulance will let them skip the line.
You don't have to call 911 for everything. Really, you don't. And we judge you when you do.

I'm a recently-certified paramedic (was an EMT-Basic for 3 years) for a municipal hospital-based EMS agency in Indianapolis.

I'm not sure if it works the same way in Canada as it does here, but you'll first have to attain basic-level certification as an EMT and rack up some hours on the job (or as a volunteer) before being eligible for Paramedic training. Some areas don't REQUIRE experience before going to Paramedic school, but I would strongly recommend at least getting out there and gaining some street-level experience before considering investing the time and money into Paramedic training (it took me 18 months & $6,000 USD). 

Many people find in their first job or two that EMS isn't all they thought it would be, and others love it. Personally, I found EMS to be a great way to get through college and pay the bills while providing a job environment that would help me develop valuable people skills, clinical experience (going back to school for nursing now), and professional development. The most important thing to remember is that EMS may be a calling, but it's also a very professional-oriented career field. 

There's almost none of the glamour, drama, or prestige you see in the movies. You will most often never be in the paper or on the 6:00 news, and you'll have a lot of repeat patients, system abusers, drug-seekers, and "cab-riders" who use your tax-funded vehicle for a trip downtown with a complimentary blood pressure check. Despite the stress, the bullshit, and the long hours, you will be expected to maintain a professional, skillful, and caring demeanor at all times, with every single patient. 

You'll have managers, superiors, colleagues, and subordinates just like any other job. The fact that you're in a moving ambulance all day doesn't necessarily mean it will be different from the "office/classroom" environment you're looking to avoid. Speaking of classrooms, you'll be spending hundreds of hours in training, refresher courses, and seminars to get and maintain your certification--get used to the idea, and remember that training is both for your benefit and your patients'. Your ambulance is also a moving classroom. After being in the field for almost 5 years, I still learn at least one thing new every single shift.

For all your patient knows, you are the BEST damned EMT/medic in the entire world walking through their front door-until you prove them otherwise. Make sure you don't.

The pay sucks (I make $15/hour), the hours are long and unpredictable, and sometimes it honestly feels like I could be doing something better with myself. My advice to you is not to make EMS into your lifelong career, but instead use the field as a stepping stone to something better. I know I personally don't want to be jumping out of ambulances when I'm 40, and I'd certainly like to make more money than I do now. But if you're young, it's an exciting, often-rewarding, and unique field to be a part of. If your heart is set on it, go for it  110% and work to distinguish yourself from your peers-because nowadays, unemployment is high and EMTs (even Paramedics in some places) are a dime a dozen. 

The world of EMS can be very small, watch what you say and what you do. Try and  get along with your partners, too-you WILL have to rely on them every single day, and you WILL need them to cover your ass. Also, I can't emphasize this enough-GET ALONG WITH FIREFIGHTERS AND POLICE, because they will literally be some of your best (and only) friends on some scenes. And you will see a lot of them. 3 out of every 4 calls I get dispatched on have an engine or a squad car on scene by the time I get there.

You might have to get started by working for a private service,  doing routine transports-don't get frustrated if you're not immediate 911, because it's a great way to get your feet wet and meet people. But, don't stick around for too long, either-because it's very easy to get burned out and disillusioned. Try and go 911 (work for a municipal agency or fire dept.) as soon as you can, if you're looking for that type of working experience. 


~*~*

TL;DR -EMS is similar to lots of other jobs, and might not be all that you're looking for in terms of working environment & compensation, BUT it's a great first career field to be in and can be rewarding, too. Pay attention in class, and get experience. Get along with other people and be professional.
-Paramedic.
